item.title: Why Should Students Write? Let Us Count the Ways.
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Writing Isn’t as Important as We Think,” by Joe Cruz, a professor at Williams College (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 1):

As a Williams alumna, as well as a novelist, I was disappointed with Professor Cruz’s argument that writing isn’t as important to students as most of us think.

Engaging fully in the writing process is, and should remain, a central tenet of liberal arts education. Why? Because it is hard. Perseverance is the point. Guiding a piece of writing from a bad first draft into a polished final product is a difficult but meaningful exercise for the mind.

My favorite professor at Williams, the great American short story writer Jim Shepard, said that drafting a written piece was like combing very tangled hair. It is slow going. You get stuck, trapped in snarls, but with patience and grit, you gradually make the hair smooth.

Now, here is a professor guiding his students to hand over the comb to the robot that will do the pesky detangling work for them.

This is poor advice. Yes, this knotty process helps us master the art of writing. But it also teaches us a much more important lesson: Frustration, pushing ourselves to the edge of failure, is the very thing that crafts us into strong, capable people.

By all means, cede a majority of the writing process to A.I. Choose the easy path. But don’t tell us that the difficult one wasn’t worth much after all.

Lauren EdmondsonHerndon, Va.

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz argues in his essay against a claim that nobody is likely to make — that students learn to think only by writing. Surely, all would agree that thinking is also aided by reading, listening and discussing.

The philosophical passage he cites that criticizes writing is from Plato, arguably the greatest of all philosophical writers. You might as well find a line from Shakespeare dismissing the importance of playwriting.

Professor Cruz notes that he doesn’t teach from prepared scripts. That observation, however, hardly implies that writing is unimportant. After all, his professorial role involves extensive writing.

Eventually, Professor Cruz admits that writing is an essential life skill, but he says nothing about how he teaches his students to write effectively. Or does he? He equates writing and archiving. Note, though, that his essay seeking to persuade is written.

Even Abraham Lincoln, one of our greatest orators and literary stylists, read the Gettysburg Address from a written script.

Steven M. CahnOld Greenwich, Conn.The writer is a professor emeritus of philosophy at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and the author of “Towards Teaching Philosophy.”

To the Editor:

As a former journalist turned entrepreneur who has long considered writing a strength, I’ve spent a lot of time wondering what A.I. will do to the craft.

I also have a high-achieving 10-year-old with dysgraphia, which for her manifests primarily as difficulty with spelling. Too often, that gets misconstrued by grade-school teachers as an inability to write or construct an organized argument. The result is that she can become reluctant to use her robust vocabulary or fully engage in writing assignments.

I’ve told her that the art of writing is really about formulating an argument, supporting it with evidence and, hopefully, engaging an audience enough so that it wants to listen.

That’s why I was so heartened by this essay and its argument for other ways to demonstrate knowledge. Quite honestly, it also reflects how most of us communicate in the working world. How many of us are regularly writing formal papers in the field or the boardroom to make a point?

Lindsay StewartNew York

To the Editor:

Reading Joe Cruz’s essay made me suspect he lacks knowledge about being an introvert. Besides needing downtime alone to recharge, introverts often need extra time for reflection and to formulate thoughts, and we do this best away from the clamor of others.

In small seminars at Wellesley College, I learned a lot from students batting ideas back and forth, and occasionally I thought quickly enough to get a word in edgewise. But for the thorniest issues, I have always done my best thinking on my own and with paper and pencil, still my best tools.

I have worked as a journalist and written children’s books. And I have led workshops for writers — in mental hospitals, jails and writing programs — where the mantra is “We write to discover what we think.”

Mary CarpenterWashington

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz has a low opinion of writing. The philosophy professor believes that conversation and debate are what best reveal deep thought, whereas writing is really “archiving” — a storage function — or “scaffolding,” a trifling utility. Elsewhere he states that writing “summarizes and compresses our thoughts,” as if it’s a zip-file option. He’s wrong.

Many smart and creative people over the years have observed that writing is thinking. Not separate from or duplicative of, but actually integral to it. As Joan Didion noted in 1976, for example, “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.”

That’s because you can’t efficiently generate, develop, organize, expand or ruminate on your ideas unless you’re committing them to the page. Even people with extraordinary memories require composition to construct deeper thoughts — not because they couldn’t remember three things, or 30, but because the process of writing necessitates the process of thinking.

Articulation requires cogitation. Or to use another metaphor, writing isn’t the frosting atop dessert; it’s the whole cake.

Joe HaydenMemphis

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz’s article on A.I. and writing in the college classroom showed a disappointing level of reasoning on two counts.

First, from my vantage as a longtime dual-enrollment college writing instructor, Professor Cruz seems blithely unaware of the scale at which most college teaching is done. He suggests 45-minute oral exam periods for a final. At the moment, I teach 90 writing students; if I followed his method, conducting finals would take 67 hours!

Professor Cruz does not mention the extent of his teaching schedule, but I suggest he more seriously consider the demands placed on the adjuncts and other typical instructors who do the majority of teaching. His system isn’t tenable when delivering instruction at scale, and the majority of college teachers (maybe not department chairs like him) are delivering at scale.

Second, I’m surprised at the professor’s use of Plato’s “Phaedrus.” Interpreting Plato always requires the reader to see the ironic, dramatic distance between Socrates, the character in Plato’s dialogues, and Plato himself, the thinker and writer. Plato chose writing to capture his thoughts. The Socratic criticism of writing in “Phaedrus” should be considered, but only as a criticism that Socrates’ best student, Plato, chose not to adopt.

William HughesCharlottesville, Va.

To the Editor:

Joe Cruz cites Plato’s hostility to writing in support of his argument. Of course, Plato didn’t have access to studies documenting important changes in brain functioning associated with writing.

On the other hand, we should have taken his warnings concerning the vulnerability of democracies to demagogues much more seriously.

Thomas W. AllenChesterfield, Mo.The writer is an emeritus associate professor of education at Washington University in St. Louis.

item.title: Abolish Frats
item.description:
The fact that Jane Doe’s assault at Cornell occurred at a fraternity house is, unfortunately, not a surprise: It is a crucial fact of the case. Greek life is associated with higher rates of sexual assault on college campuses. Studies have shown fraternity members are three times as likely to commit sexual assault as other male students. Sorority women are 74 percent more likely to be sexually assaulted than other college women. For all these reasons and more, as undergraduates at American University, we led a movement to abolish fraternities and sororities.

Our fight for change didn’t work. Our story shows how challenging it is.

In 2020, the four of us started our college experience from our childhood bedrooms, because of the pandemic. Amid this exciting new chapter of our lives, we noticed several Instagram accounts popping up that featured A.U. students and alumni sharing their troubling experiences of racial discrimination, sexual abuse and brutal hazing, many of which occurred in and around social Greek life. A.U. has a reputation for having a progressive student body, and these testimonies troubled many of us in the freshman class. In many of the class of 2024’s GroupMe chats, discussions often revolved around how ridiculous it was that the things we read about were allowed to occur with no adequate response from the university. The four of us became friends because of our shared political perspectives, connections that we built digitally via Facebook posts and online group chats.

Many undergraduates we knew swore off Greek life and found it unacceptable that the university continued to allow its existence. Abby had initially considered joining a sorority: She had seen the cute Instagram photos of sisterhood and matching outfits. But after reading the testimonials of Greek life on A.U.’s campus, she quickly decided against it. All of us felt viscerally that if one member of our campus could be harmed and devalued, then the same thing could happen to any of us.

When we finally arrived on campus in 2021, we saw fraternities with recruitment tables on the quad. We watched some of the same classmates who had discussed the violence of fraternities on GroupMe flock to them, in search of some semblance of in-person community. We doubt that the chess club would ever be allowed to recruit on campus if statistically its members were three times as likely to commit sexual assault as the general student body. Why did this double standard exist for fraternities?

Abby and Olivia were roommates, and they printed fliers that read: “Do you like racism? Do you enjoy misogyny? Well, then joining Greek life is for you!” But posting them freely wasn’t allowed. So we attempted to form a club called “Abolish Greek Life at A.U.” With club status, we would be allowed to table on the quad, put up fliers, host events, and receive funding. We felt that we were addressing a just cause that our fellow students and our liberal university would welcome with open arms.

Our application to become a club was denied. We would be permitted to exist as a formal club only if we changed our mission from abolishing Greek life to merely reforming it. We refused.

Turning to social media, we posted statistics and student testimonials on Instagram. We saw lots of comments in support of our posts, which ranged from infographics on how Greek life protects abusers to a statement of support in response to comments made on social media about an alleged sexual assault by a member of a fraternity. However, we also saw plenty of hate — other students would often mock us, or post hate comments. Others accused us of being performative or exaggerating what was a big state school issue, not an issue at A.U.

But we had our allies. We organized with members of the student government, and in the spring of 2022, we got two referendum questions on the campuswide ballot. To achieve this, we attended lengthy student government meetings that sometimes took up our entire Saturdays. We recall being criticized by members of the student government, who didn’t know we were within earshot. We persuaded other A.U. clubs to co-sign our fliers about the referendum so that we could post them throughout campus. A large piece of our campaign was talking to our fellow students and trying to get them to join our cause. Many of them told us that they were uncomfortable with the behavior of Greek life organizations but that they were desperate for social infrastructure. Though abolishing fraternities and sororities was our main goal, we realized the importance of creating alternative forms of community for A.U. students.

When the results were tallied, 46 percent of voting students said they did not support the presence of Greek life on campus, compared with 41 percent who said they did. Even more clearly, 73 percent of students said they desired alternatives to Greek life that would help build community on A.U.’s campus.

Amid the aftermath of the referendums, the director of A.U.’s Center for Student Involvement told the campus newspaper that the university “would not recognize any club whose goal was to abolish another student involvement opportunity on campus.” Ultimately, despite all our efforts, nothing happened.

Greek life throughout the country has been given opportunities to reform, yet horrific incidents happen time and time again. Why don’t more universities consider abolishing frats? We believe part of it is money. Nationwide, university alumni who were members of Greek life are far likelier than their non-Greek counterparts to donate to their institution — with one survey showing 54 percent of those who went Greek donating to their alma mater, as opposed to the 10 percent of nonaffiliated alumni. This suggests to us that universities have a financial incentive to ignore the sexual abuse, hazing and discrimination that Greek life perpetuates.

We recognize the need for social networks and support systems on college campuses. But there are ample examples of alternative communities on campuses across the country. Many colleges and universities — including Rice, Notre Dame, Colby, Alfred, Amherst — have either abolished their Greek systems, or never let them take root at all. Some people might find us naïve, but we still believe just as firmly that abolition, not reform, is the only answer. These other schools serve as models: We don’t need to imagine something new to imagine something better.

Parthav Easwar works in environmental policy in Washington. Bella Paracca is a museum professional and a writer based in Pittsburgh. Abby Sharkis is a political researcher based in Washington. Olivia O’Connor is a writer and a teacher based in Massachusetts.

item.title: Why Ketamine Immobilizes Some Users
item.description: Ketamine is a useful sedative and antidepressant at light doses. At stronger doses, it is a powerful anesthetic, but at repeated high doses, it deadens sensation, leaving users conscious but unable to act. ]]>
